questions.q: What does confirmation bias lead people to do?
a: Seek out information that supports what they already believe
Take credit for successes while denying blame for failures
Stick with familiar choices even when better options exist
Spend most of their time on tasks with little payoff
questions.why: Lesson 1 describes confirmation bias as our tendency to look for evidence that backs up existing beliefs.

a: Claiming success for yourself but refusing blame for failure
Judging others more harshly than you judge yourself
Believing you are less biased than everyone around you
Preferring the default option whenever one is offered
questions.why: Lesson 1 explains that the self-serving bias makes us own good outcomes and disown bad ones.

questions.q: According to the summary, why do people cling to the status quo?
a: It saves energy and feels safer than the unknown
It always produces better results over time
It protects them from every cognitive bias
It is required by most employers and families
questions.why: Lesson 2 says we avoid change because we are wired to conserve energy and weigh losses heavily.

questions.q: How does the Pareto principle describe the link between effort and results?
a: A small portion of causes generates most of the outcome
Effort and results always rise at the same rate
Most results come from luck rather than deliberate work
Only measurable tasks produce any real results
questions.why: Lesson 3 presents the 80/20 rule: roughly 80 percent of outcomes stem from 20 percent of causes.

questions.q: When you feel like turning down an opportunity, what should you ask yourself?
a: Am I avoiding this out of comfort or because I truly don't want it?
Is this the cheapest option available to me right now?
Would my friends and family approve of this choice?
Can I finish this before the end of the week?
questions.why: Lesson 2 recommends checking whether the pull of the familiar, rather than genuine disinterest, is driving your answer.
